name: Sandworm Team
summary: A Russian GRU Unit 74455 threat group responsible for destructive global operations and multiple attacks that produced or attempted operational effects in Ukraine's electric grid.

assessment.text: Sandworm has demonstrated the full path from enterprise intrusion to deliberate physical-process disruption, combining patient access, legitimate operator functionality, purpose-built ICS malware and destructive recovery inhibition.

The group's operations are global, but Ukraine remains the central proving ground for electric-grid attacks, wipers and operationally coordinated cyber activity supporting Russian military objectives.
BadPilot illustrates the access layer behind destructive capability: scalable perimeter exploitation and persistent access may precede a later high-impact operation by months or years.

Sandworm's OT effect tooling is trending toward less code and faster deployment: a four-protocol framework in 2016, a single IEC-104 binary with hardcoded targets in 2022, then native SCADA functionality with no custom ICS malware in October 2022.

Initial access is the least evidenced phase of the grid campaigns. Only 2015 has a confirmed vector (spearphishing with macro-bearing Office documents); 2016 is assessed as likely phishing, and neither 2022 intrusion has a publicly identified vector. Dossier claims about entry for those campaigns are inference, not confirmation.

Every documented grid intrusion entered through the enterprise IT estate and worked toward OT, typically via dual-homed hosts, shared Active Directory identity or remote access paths. The IT-to-OT pivot, not the PLC or RTU, is the decisive detection point.

Dwell time between enterprise access and OT impact is measured in months: roughly six months in 2015, between two and eleven months in 2016, and around four months in October 2022, where Mandiant assessed the attacker may have held SCADA access for up to three months and developed the OT capability as late as three weeks before the outage.

ESET's 2018 discovery of the Exaramel backdoor supplied the first code-level link between Industroyer and the TeleBots activity behind BlackEnergy and NotPetya, consolidating separate campaigns under one operator.

campaigns.name: 2015 Ukraine electric-power attack
campaigns.summary: Spearphishing emails carrying macro-bearing Microsoft Office documents installed the BlackEnergy 3 toolkit at three electricity distribution companies. Months of enterprise access and credential harvesting culminated on 23 December in remote use of operator workstations to open breakers at roughly 30 substations, overwrite serial-to-Ethernet device firmware and inhibit recovery. This is the only grid campaign with a publicly confirmed initial access vector.
campaigns.impact: Approximately 225,000 customers lost power; operators restored service manually while call centers and remote control were disrupted.

campaigns.name: 2016 Ukraine electric-power attack
campaigns.summary: Industroyer/CrashOverride automated interaction with electric-grid protocols and issued commands to a transmission substation in Kyiv on 17 December. Initial access was never publicly confirmed; the intrusion may have begun with phishing as early as January 2016, with IT network access evidenced no later than October 2016. The attackers used valid accounts, living-off-the-land techniques, PsExec and Mimikatz to traverse the enterprise, pivoted into the ICS network via a likely dual-homed host, and reached Windows Server 2003 SQL Server systems assessed as data historians before reaching equipment-facing hosts.
campaigns.impact: Part of Kyiv lost power for roughly an hour, and the operation demonstrated reusable, protocol-aware ICS attack capability.

campaigns.name: NotPetya
campaigns.summary: A compromised M.E.Doc update distributed a destructive wiper disguised as ransomware, which propagated rapidly through enterprise networks.
campaigns.impact: Global collateral damage disrupted shipping, logistics, pharmaceuticals and other sectors; the U.S. indictment cites nearly one billion dollars in losses among three victims alone.

campaigns.name: Industroyer2 attempt
campaigns.summary: A targeted IEC-104 payload built from the original Industroyer source was scheduled against Ukrainian high-voltage substations alongside Windows, Linux and Solaris wipers. Target IP addresses, ASDU addresses and information object addresses were hardcoded into the binary rather than read from a configuration file. CERT-UA reported the initial compromise occurred no later than February 2022; the entry vector was not identified publicly.
campaigns.impact: Defenders disrupted the attempt before the planned power interruption; the operation showed refined, target-specific ICS execution.

campaigns.name: October 2022 MicroSCADA living-off-the-land outage
campaigns.summary: No custom ICS malware was used. The attacker executed a native MicroSCADA binary, scilc.exe, from an ISO image mounted on the hypervisor hosting the victim's SCADA management instance, issuing commands that opened breakers. The intrusion began on or before June 2022, with SCADA access assessed as possibly held for up to three months and the OT capability potentially developed as late as three weeks before execution. Mandiant could not identify the initial access vector.
campaigns.impact: An unscheduled power outage at a Ukrainian substation, timed to coincide with Russian missile strikes on Ukrainian cities; CaddyWiper was deployed across the IT estate two days later to compound disruption and destroy forensic evidence.

campaigns.name: BadPilot global access operation
campaigns.summary: A multiyear access campaign exploited perimeter products at scale, established persistence, harvested credentials and expanded from Ukraine to organisations across several continents.
campaigns.impact: Long-lived access provides espionage value and can establish the conditions for later destructive operations.

capabilities.name: Operate industrial processes through intended functionality
capabilities.description: Use SCADA interfaces and protocol-valid commands to manipulate breakers and deny operator control.

capabilities.name: Develop purpose-built ICS malware
capabilities.description: Create reusable frameworks and target-specific payloads that communicate with electric-power equipment.

capabilities.name: Destroy enterprise and recovery infrastructure
capabilities.description: Deploy wipers, modify firmware, disable tooling and coordinate data destruction with operational effects.

capabilities.name: Cause OT impact with native platform tooling
capabilities.description: Execute vendor-supplied SCADA binaries and scripting interfaces already present on control hosts, removing the need for custom ICS malware and shrinking the detectable footprint.

capabilities.name: Pivot from enterprise IT into control networks
capabilities.description: Traverse the corporate estate with valid accounts, credential dumping and living-off-the-land tooling, then cross into OT through dual-homed hosts, shared domain identity or remote access paths.

capabilities.name: Sustain long pre-impact dwell in OT environments
capabilities.description: Hold access for months while learning the process environment and equipment addressing, then build or configure an effect capability specific to the plant shortly before execution.

capabilities.name: Acquire persistent access at scale
capabilities.description: Exploit exposed perimeter products, deploy web shells and remote tools, and collect credentials for later tasking.

malware.name: BlackEnergy 3 and KillDisk
malware.description: Enterprise intrusion and destructive components used around the 2015 Ukraine power operation.

malware.name: Industroyer / CrashOverride
malware.description: A modular ICS framework with four protocol payloads (IEC-101, IEC-104, IEC-61850 and OPC DA), a main backdoor, a second backdoor hidden in a trojanised Notepad application and a wiper component, capable of automating operational disruption at substation equipment.

malware.name: Exaramel
malware.description: A backdoor whose code-level similarity to Industroyer's main backdoor gave the first public evidence tying Industroyer to the TeleBots group behind BlackEnergy and NotPetya.

malware.name: scilc.exe (native MicroSCADA utility)
malware.description: A legitimate vendor binary abused to run SCIL commands against substation equipment in October 2022, delivered via an ISO mounted on the SCADA host's hypervisor.
malware.caveat: Not attacker-authored. Detection must key on anomalous invocation of trusted platform tooling rather than file reputation.

malware.name: NotPetya
malware.description: A destructive wiper masquerading as ransomware that spread globally from a compromised Ukrainian software update.

malware.name: Industroyer2
malware.description: A streamlined IEC-104 payload configured for a targeted 2022 attempt against Ukrainian substations.

malware.name: CaddyWiper / ORCSHRED / SOLOSHRED / AWFULSHRED
malware.description: Destructive payloads for Windows, Linux and Solaris coordinated with the Industroyer2 attempt, with CaddyWiper reused across the IT estate two days after the October 2022 outage to compound disruption and destroy forensic evidence.

enterprise.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
enterprise.behaviour: Malicious Office and archive attachments established footholds, including in the 2015 power campaign. Lures are tailored to the recipient's role and to current events, and the 2020 indictment records the same pattern against election, Olympic, Novichok-investigation and Georgian government targets.

enterprise.name: User Execution: Malicious File
enterprise.behaviour: Recipients opened weaponised Word documents and enabled macros, which downloaded and installed the BlackEnergy 3 backdoor.

enterprise.name: Valid Accounts
enterprise.behaviour: Harvested credentials were reused for months of low-signal movement through the enterprise estate and for reaching systems bridging IT and OT.

enterprise.name: OS Credential Dumping
enterprise.behaviour: Mimikatz and comparable tooling harvested credentials to expand access toward control-network paths.

enterprise.name: System Services: Service Execution
enterprise.behaviour: PsExec and similar administrative utilities executed payloads remotely, keeping activity within expected administrative behaviour.

enterprise.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
enterprise.behaviour: PowerShell supported credential harvesting, deployment and destructive tooling.

enterprise.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
enterprise.behaviour: Administrative shares and remote services moved payloads through enterprise networks.

enterprise.name: Data Destruction
enterprise.behaviour: NotPetya and coordinated wipers rendered systems and recovery infrastructure inoperable.

enterprise.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
enterprise.behaviour: BadPilot exploited multiple enterprise perimeter products to establish scalable, persistent access.

ics.name: External Remote Services
ics.behaviour: Valid accounts and remote services provided access to operator and control environments.

ics.name: Graphical User Interface
ics.behaviour: Attackers operated SCADA/HMI interfaces to issue breaker commands during the 2015 attack.

ics.name: Block Serial COM
ics.behaviour: Firmware on serial-to-Ethernet converters was overwritten to sever downstream communications.

ics.name: Scripting
ics.behaviour: A native MicroSCADA utility ran attacker-supplied SCIL commands from an ISO mounted on the hosting hypervisor, achieving process impact without custom ICS malware.

ics.name: Default Credentials
ics.behaviour: Weak boundaries between enterprise and control identity, including shared domain accounts and flat segmentation, eased the pivot into process networks.

ics.name: Data Destruction
ics.behaviour: Wipers were deployed after or alongside process impact to obstruct recovery and destroy forensic evidence, including CaddyWiper two days after the October 2022 outage.

ics.name: Unauthorized Command Message
ics.behaviour: Protocol-valid commands were issued to electric substation equipment.

ics.name: Denial of Control
ics.behaviour: Device and communication sabotage denied operators reliable downstream control.

ics.name: Loss of Availability
ics.behaviour: Breaker operations and destructive actions interrupted electric service and system availability.

ics.name: Loss of Control
ics.behaviour: Operators lost remote control and relied on manual restoration procedures.

ics.name: Manipulation of Control
ics.behaviour: Breaker states and operational commands were deliberately altered to disrupt the grid.

indicatorNotice: This dossier prioritises durable behaviour over historical campaign infrastructure. Sandworm routinely changes access infrastructure and reuses legitimate services; point-in-time indicators should remain tied to the source campaign and collection date.

defensivePriorities.name: Separate process control from enterprise identity failure
defensivePriorities.description: Enforce strong segmentation, dedicated OT identities, controlled jump paths and independent operator authentication.

defensivePriorities.name: Detect valid but abnormal control actions
defensivePriorities.description: Baseline breaker operations, engineering changes and IEC-104 command sequences; alert on commands that are technically valid but operationally unexpected.

defensivePriorities.name: Protect restoration and manual operations
defensivePriorities.description: Maintain offline recovery, tested manual control, independent communications and rehearsed black-start or degraded-mode procedures.

defensivePriorities.name: Hunt perimeter access as pre-attack activity
defensivePriorities.description: Treat exploitation, web shells, OWA credential collection and new remote tools as potential preparation for later destructive tasking.

defensivePriorities.name: Instrument the IT-to-OT pivot as the primary chokepoint
defensivePriorities.description: Inventory dual-homed hosts, historians and engineering workstations, separate OT identity from the corporate domain, and alert on any enterprise-originated authentication or file transfer crossing into the control network.

defensivePriorities.name: Alert on native SCADA tooling used outside normal operations
defensivePriorities.description: Baseline execution of vendor utilities on control hosts, and treat unexpected invocation, mounted ISO or removable images on SCADA hypervisors, and out-of-band scripting as high-severity events even when the binary is signed and legitimate.

defensivePriorities.name: Harden and monitor the phishing entry path for OT-adjacent staff
defensivePriorities.description: Block or restrict macros in documents from the internet, apply attachment detonation, and prioritise engineers, control-room staff and anyone handling operational documentation for phishing-resistant authentication and targeted awareness.

defensivePriorities.name: Contain coordinated wiper deployment
defensivePriorities.description: Protect domain controllers, software distribution, hypervisors and backups from shared administrative paths and Group Policy abuse.
